b: A Minnesota angler landed a fish that is now listed among the state’s most impressive catches. Alejanaro Garcia of Richfield, Minnesota, caught a massive 54-inch longnose gar from the Mississippi River in Winona County on Sept. 6, 2026, setting a new Minnesota state catch-and-release record.

The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (DNR) confirmed the record in November, recognizing Garcia’s fish as being three inches longer than the previous state record. The state’s existing certified-weight record for longnose gar remains a 16-pound, 12-ounce, fish caught in 1982 from the St. Croix River near Prescott. That fish measured 53 inches, one shy of Garcia’s fish.
Longnose Gar: A Fish From Another Era
Longnose gar, like these specimens in a Georgia Aquarium, are relics of the past. Courtesy Wikipedia

Few North American freshwater fish look as prehistoric as the longnose gar. With its elongated body, narrow tooth-filled jaws, and armor-like scales, the species appears almost unchanged from an ancient aquatic world.

There is a good reason for that appearance. Gar have a fossil history extending back more than 100 million years, and modern representatives retain several distinctive anatomical characteristics associated with their ancient lineage.

Longnose gar belong to the family Lepisosteidae. They are not primitive or unevolved fish, but rather a highly specialized group that has successfully maintained a distinctive body design over an enormous span of geological time.

One of the most recognizable characteristics of a longnose gar is its protective covering. Its body is shielded by hard, diamond-shaped scales called ganoid scales. These scales contain a dense, enamel-like outer layer that provides substantial protection against both injury and predators.

Unlike the flexible scales found on many familiar sport fish, gar scales form an exceptionally tough exterior. This natural armor is one reason gar have such a distinctive appearance — and have survived in freshwater environments for millions of years.

The longnose gar’s most obvious feature is its elongated snout. Its narrow jaws contain numerous sharp, needle-like teeth designed to grasp and hold prey. Rather than swallowing large fish whole through a wide-opening mouth, longnose gar generally capture smaller fish with quick sideways strikes.

They are primarily fish-eating predators, although their diet can include insects and other aquatic organisms when opportunities arise. Gar are often observed near the surface, where they can remain relatively motionless before making a sudden movement to capture prey.

Perhaps the most fascinating adaptation of longnose gar is their ability to breathe air. In addition to using their gills, gar possess a highly vascularized swim bladder that functions as an accessory breathing organ.

They periodically rise to the surface and gulp air, allowing them to survive in warm, oxygen-poor water that would be challenging for many other fish species. This adaptation makes them particularly well suited to backwaters, shallow wetlands, and slow-moving river environments during periods of high temperatures and reduced dissolved oxygen.
Gar in Minnesota: An Underrated River Fishery
Longnose gar can be difficult to hook because of the unique shape of their mouths. Courtesy Wikipedia
At 4 feet, 6 inches, in length, Garcia’s gar is an impressive reminder that the Land of 10,000 Lakes has more than just walleye, northern pike, bass, and muskellunge.

Minnesota is home to two native gar species: the longnose gar (Lepisosteus osseus) and the shortnose gar (Lepisosteus platostomus). Both species are primarily associated with the state’s larger river systems, particularly the Mississippi, St. Croix, and Minnesota rivers, along with some of their tributaries.

Longnose gar generally favor warm, relatively slow-moving water. Backwaters, oxbow lakes, flooded vegetation, and quiet river margins provide important habitat. The Mississippi River around southeastern Minnesota is particularly suitable for gar, with an extensive network of backwaters, side channels, and connected wetlands. These environments offer plenty of feeding opportunities and spawning areas.

Shortnose gar also inhabit these river systems, although their appearance differs somewhat from their longnose relatives. Longnose gar have a noticeably longer, narrower snout, while shortnose gar have a shorter and broader snout.

Gar have historically been classified as rough fish, and they have sometimes been unfairly blamed for reducing populations of more desirable sport fish. Modern understanding recognizes their ecological importance as native predators and members of a complex aquatic food web.

Minnesota’s DNR began a comprehensive gar research effort in 2022 to improve its understanding of these species and their status within the state. Interestingly, Minnesota DNR research has also highlighted their importance as host fish for certain freshwater mussels.

Although gar are not generally considered a sport fish in Minnesota, their size, fighting ability, and unusual appearance make them a good target for anglers looking to pursue something different. To get an idea of just how big, take a look at some of the biggest gar records ever caught.
